list.listitem: Tinea corporis, cruris, and pedis are diagnosed by typical historical and physical findings. The diagnosis may be confirmed by KOH preparation and/or fungal culture. C
Topical medications should be the first line of treatment. Topical terbinafine and all azoles have been shown to be safe and effective for treatment of tinea corporis, cruris, and pedis. A
Oral medications should be reserved for severe cases or when topical treatments have failed. B
Oral itraconazole, fluconazole, and terbinafine are safe and effective for the treatment of tinea corporis, cruris, and pedis. B

background.definition: Tinea corporis, or "ringworm," is the term used for a dermatophyte infection of the glabrous skin of the trunk, legs or arms. Tinea cruris, or "jock itch," is the term used for dermatophyte infection of the groin, thighs, or perineal region. Tinea pedis, or "athlete's foot," is the term used for dermatophyte infection of the feet.

list.listitem: Superficial fungal infections are believed to affect 20-25% of the world’s population.
Tinea pedis is the most common dermatophytosis; about 15% of the population have fungal infection of the feet.
The global cost of treating dermatophytes is estimated to cost five hundred million dollars annually (four hundred million dollars annually in the United States).
Dermatophytoses can be acquired through contact with infected people, animals, and soil.
Tinea corporis, cruris and pedis may result from spread from onychomycosis.
Tinea corporis occurs more commonly before puberty; tinea cruris occurs more commonly after puberty.
Causative agents for tinea corporis and cruris are Trichophyton rubrum (32%-60%), Trichophyton tonsurans (17.7%-34.3%), and Candida species (<24%).
Trichophyton rubrum causes most tinea pedis and onychomycosis.
Dermatophytes invade susceptible skin and persist at the level of the stratum corneum.
Skin response to the infection includes proliferation, scaling, and epidermal thickening.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Exposure to other infected individuals (any type of tinea)
Increased perspiration often due to athletics or physical activity

list.listitem: Diagnosis is based on key historical and physical findings (erythema, scaling, central clearing, pruritus) and may be confirmed with KOH preparation and/or fungal skin culture. C
Skin biopsy and bacterial cultures may be helpful in ruling out other disease processes or confirming bacterial superinfection. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually not annular; history of exposure to contact allergen; negative KOH preparation
History of similar eruptions in past; distribution along flexor surfaces; negative KOH preparation
Scaling plaques on extensor surfaces; negative KOH preparation
Typical distribution on scalp and face; greasy scale that is not annular; negative KOH preparation
Characteristic eruption that follows skin tension lines; often has herald patch; lesions have fine collarette scale; negative KOH preparation
Hypo- or hyperpigmented macules and patches with fine scale on the upper trunk; "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance on KOH preparation
May be annular but will have a negative KOH preparation; punch biopsy needed to confirm this diagnosis
One or more raised rings without scale on the fingers, hands, elbows, dorsal feet, or ankles; negative KOH preparation
Most often in the groin or axillae; may show coral red fluorescence with UV light
Scale and small vesicles on the hands and feet
Active athletic lifestyle, no macerations, cracks or fissures
Annular plaque with trailing rim of scale

list.listitem: Tinea corporis/cruris typically presents as an erythematous, annular plaque, with well-defined margins. Lesions tend to have a scale and expand concentrically and have central clearing. The lesions may be pruritic or macerated.

Tinea pedis often presents as interdigital white or green fungal growth between the toes with erythema, cracks, fissures and/or maceration or scale. Vesicles or bullae may be present. Lesions sometimes ulcerate. Onychomycosis is often present.
Assess duration of condition, previous occurrences, current and previous treatments, and presence of other skin diseases.

The history should screen for risk factors such as hepatic disease, renal disease, immunocompromised state, endocrine disease, and the use of systemic medications. Briefly review any occupational, environmental, and recreational exposure (eg, work with animals, new pets, contact sports, use of sports facilities, gardening, and soil exposure).

The best predictors of onychomycosis (similar in accuracy to a dermatologist's examination) are plantar desquamation and the presence of interdigital tinea pedis. Other significant factors include a previous diagnosis of fungal disease in the feet and subungual hyperkeratosis.

KOH preparation can be readily done in the office to observe characteristic septate hyphae. Using a mixture of KOH, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and a fungal stain may make it easier to find the hyphae under the microscope (sensitivity 88%, specificity 95%, positive predictive value 73%, negative predictive value 98%). Another test with higher sensitivity is using cyanoacrylate adhesive to remove a sheet of cells from the stratum corneum of the lesion.
Fungal culture, typically on Sabouraud glucose agar, is the reference standard.
Skin biopsy is occasionally needed to rule out other skin conditions.
Bacterial culture may be helpful if bacterial infection or superinfection is suspected.
In severe cases, bullae or vesicles may need to be drained.

A Wood's light (UV light) may be helpful to detect tinea caused by Microsporum species (which will appear blue green or dull yellow). However, most tinea infections are now due to Trichophyton and will not fluoresce. Erythrasma, a superficial bacterial infection due to Corynebacterium minutissimum, may show coral red fluorescence in UV light.
The history and physical examination is often enough to secure the diagnosis of tinea corporis or tinea cruris. The diagnosis can be verified with a KOH preparation.
Once the diagnosis is established, topical therapy can be instituted if the lesion is small, if significant hyperkeratinization is not seen, or if the lesion does not involve the palms.

If the lesion is extensive, the patient has failed topical therapy, or if the patient is immunocompromised, oral therapy should be considered, unless there is a contraindication such as severe liver disease.
Topical medications should be the first line of treatment. Topical terbinafine and all azoles have been shown to be safe and effective for treatment of tinea corporis, cruris, and pedis. A
Oral agents should be reserved for severe cases or in cases that have failed to respond to topical therapy. B
Oral itraconazole, fluconazole, and terbinafine are safe and effective for the treatment of tinea corporis, cruris, and pedis. B

Topical therapy may be effective in cases that are not severe or widespread. A Cochrane review found allylamines (e.g., terbinafine) and azoles to have higher cure rates than placebo for tinea pedis, with allylamines slightly more effective than azoles, with a treatment failure risk ratio of 0.63 (95% CI, 0.42-0.94).

A Cochrane review evaluating topical therapies for tinea cruris and tinea corporis, including 129 studies comprising 18,086 participants, demonstrated no difference in mycological cure between topical azoles and benzylamines (e.g., butenafine), although data was not able to be pooled due to study heterogeneity to assess clinical cure rates. Individual treatment with terbinafine and naftifine appear effective, with minimal adverse events (e.g., burning, local irritation). Combination of topical steroids and antifungals may have slightly higher clinical cure rate than topical antifungals alone, but mycological cure rates appear comparable between the two groups at the end of therapy (very low-quality evidence).

One study (n = 65) showed that a 1% emulsion gel of terbinafine applied daily for 1 week was superior to ketoconazole 2% cream applied daily for 2 weeks in terms to mycologic cure (94% vs 69%, p = 0.027) for tinea cruris and tinea corporis. A 7-day course of terbinafine has been found to be more effective than placebo in achieving and maintaining mycologic cure rate (84.2% vs 23.3%, p <.001) for tinea cruris and corporis.

Butenafine 1% cream applied daily for 2 weeks is a safe and effective treatment for tinea cruris. Butenafine 1% cream was superior to placebo beginning at day 7 of a 14-day treatment for tinea corporis. At day 42, the butenafine treatment group had a response rate of 81% vs 14% for vehicle control. In another study, butenafine 1% cream once daily for 2 weeks was superior to clotrimazole 1% twice daily for 4 weeks in clinical cure at the end of 1 week for tinea cruris and corporis. The difference in clinical cure was not clinically significant at 4 and 8 weeks of treatment.

Using 10 years of data from the National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey and National Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (1995-2004), one study found that ineffective treatment of tinea pedis, tinea corporis, and tinea cruris with nystatin commonly occurred. Nystatin is adequate treatment for candida and not tinea.

Systemic therapy may be needed if the patient cannot tolerate topical treatment, if the involved area is extensive, if hyperkeratosis is pronounced, if patients have chronic infection, if topical therapy has failed, or if the patient is immunocompromised. Options include terbinafine, itraconazole, fluconazole, and griseofulvin.

Itraconazole 100 mg daily for 2 weeks was found to be safe and effective in the treatment of tinea corporis and tinea cruris (96% of lesions were healed or improved versus 39% in the placebo group; 57% mycologic cure rate versus 17% in placebo group). Itraconazole 200 mg daily for 1 week was found to be similarly effective, as well tolerated, and as safe as 100 mg daily for 2 weeks. Another study found that 100 mg of itraconazole daily for 15 days was superior to 500 mg of oral griseofulvin daily for 15 days in terms to mycologic cure rate.

A small study of children with tinea corporis and cruris (n = 15) found that itraconazole at a dose of 5 mg/kg/d was a safe and effective treatment (clinical cure rate of 100%; mycologic cure rate of 93%).
A total of 400 mg/day was found to be the minimal effective dose of itraconazole. This study also used topical antifungals.

Fluconazole 150 mg once weekly for 2 to 4 weeks appears to be safe and effective in the treatment of tinea corporis and tinea cruris. There was no significant statistical difference in outcomes in patients treated with fluconazole 50 mg/day versus fluconazole 150 mg once weekly. Another study found that fluconazole 150 mg once weekly for 4 to 6 weeks was as effective as griseofulvin 500 mg once daily for 4 to 6 weeks (74% vs 64% mycologic cure rate). Adverse treatment-related events were 7.5% for fluconazole and 12.5% for griseofulvin.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) warns against the use of oral ketoconazole due to the risk of fatal liver injury, drug interactions, and QT prolongation.

Oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 2 weeks was equivalent to griseofulvin 500 mg daily for 2 weeks. At 6-week follow-up, oral terbinafine was superior to griseofulvin is mycologic cure rate and clinical response. Terbinafine had a lower relapse rate than griseofulvin.

A systematic review of 17 randomized controlled trials including 3798 patients compared amphotericin B versus fluconazole in the treatment of fungal infections in neutropenic cancer patients. Intravenous amphotericin B was the only antifungal agent to reduce mortality. It was noted that the studies demonstrated bias against amphotericin B in either design or analysis.
The preferred treatment of dermatophytosis in children, pregnant women, and the elderly is with topical azoles and allylamines.
Oral terbinafine and itraconazole are safe for use in children and the elderly.
All oral antifungal agents should be avoided in pregnancy and during breastfeeding.
Skin biopsy may be occasionally needed when the diagnosis is unclear or to rule out other diagnoses.

One small study (n = 70, divided into four groups) showed that oil of bitter orange preparations led to faster response rates (33% cure rate at 1 week) than imidazole preparations. This was a non-randomized study with a high drop-out rate.
Avoidance of predisposing factors (animals, soil, gym equipment, etc.).
Photodynamic therapy is less effective than azole therapy for treatment of tinea pedis and cruris, however may have utility in treatment of other fungal infections .
Referral is indicated for severe cases, cases that fail to respond to conventional therapy, or cases for which the diagnosis is uncertain.
Antibiotics may be helpful if bacterial superinfection exists.
Although topical and oral treatments are very effective, recurrence rates can be high. If significant hyperkeratosis exists, lesions can last for weeks or months. C
Follow-up is determined by the extent of disease, the length of treatment, the type of treatment, and clinical response. C
Skin lesions can last weeks to months and can last even longer if there is significant hyperkeratosis present.
Recurrence is common, although data on the recurrence rate are not available.
The frequency of follow-up is determined by the extent and severity of disease as well as the response to therapy.

While baseline AST, ALT, and CBC are recommended prior to the initiation of oral griseofulvin and terbinafine, it may not be necessary to continue to monitor these levels in otherwise healthy patients. A retrospective cohort study of 4985 adults and children who had received 4309 courses of terbinafine and 793 courses of griseofulvin, found for both drugs, the rate of abnormal AST or ALT either at baseline or during treatment was approximately 3%. Less than 0.2% reported grade 2 or worse elevations (> 3 times the upper limit of normal) with only 1 patient discontinuing treatment as a result of hepatoxicity.
Allow affected areas to dry completely before covering with clothes.
Consider use of moisture-wicking clothes for better moisture management.
Avoid going barefoot in public showers or locker rooms.
Consider using topical medication 1-2 days after rash resolution to prevent relapse.
